newsitem.title: USA: Conn. committee OKs electric deregulation bill.
newsitem.headline: Conn. committee OKs electric deregulation bill.

text.p: A Connecticut legislative committee approved a bill on Tuesday that would allow consumers to choose their electric company.
The bill, approved by the Energy and Technology Committee, would set up a pilot program to allow 20 percent of customers to select their electric company in 1999.
All customers would be able to choose their suppliers on July 1, 2000.
The proposal must now be approved by the state's Environment Committee in order to be considered by the House of Representatives.
Connecticut's two biggest power suppliers are Northeast Utilities subsidiary Connecticut Light & Power Co, which has 1.1 million customers, and United Illuminating Co, which serves 309,000 customers.
Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal hailed the committee's passage of the bill.
"This is a bold and historic step for all of Connecticut," Blumenthal said in a statement. "With this proposal, consumers and businesses will see lower rates and enjoy the benefits of competition.

"The proposal guarantees a minimum rate decrease of 10 percent, but also gives my office the power to seek even greater consumer benefits as we carefully evaluate the costs our utilities are seeking to recover from ratepayers," Blumenthal said.
"We must work to ensure that ratepayers are not saddled with any of the costs of mismanagement by our electric companies."
Connecticut's existing power companies have said they are concerned about recovering their so-called stranded costs after deregulation.
Stranded costs are typically linked to power plants built prior to market deregulation, when their costs could be passed on through the rates utilities charged to their customers.
Connecticut utilities have stranded costs of about $4.6 billion, according to a report by Nuveen Research.

The bill, approved by a 17-1 margin by the committee on Tuesday, proposes that the award of stranded cost reimbursement cannot be so generous to the point that it gives one company an unfair competitive edge over the other companies.
It also says that the award of stranded cost reimbursement cannot be so low to the point that it undermines the financial viability of a company.
It proposes that companies will recover a "certain portion" of their stranded costs, but will not be reimbursed for investment money lost through poor management or inefficiencies.
